title: Judges 5:24–31
context: Judges 5:24–31 closes the song. Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, is blessed for killing Sisera with a tent peg as he lies at her feet, matching the prose account in 4:17–22. The scene then shifts to Sisera’s mother waiting at the window while her ladies imagine plunder and captive women. The song ends with a prayer that the LORD’s enemies perish and those who love him shine like the rising sun, and the land has rest forty years. Both traditions read Jael’s act within the song’s frame of holy war against an oppressor. They do not celebrate violence for its own sake, and they acknowledge the moral questions readers raise, including her breach of the peace between her household and Jabin (4:17).

verses.text: “Jael shall be blessed above women, the wife of Heber the Kenite; blessed shall she be above women in the tent.
verses.arminianNotes: Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, is to be blessed above women in the tent. Arminian readers read the blessing within the song’s frame: Jael sided with Israel against an oppressor. They also take seriously that the act involved deception and violence and do not hold it up as a pattern to imitate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the blessing as praise for her role in God’s deliverance rather than approval of every part of her conduct, noting that her household had been at peace with Jabin (4:17). Both traditions recognize interpreters’ ongoing discussion of the moral questions and avoid celebrating brutality for its own sake.

verses.text: He asked for water. She gave him milk. She brought him butter in a lordly dish.
verses.arminianNotes: Sisera asked for water, and she gave him milk and brought curds in a lordly dish. Arminian readers see the hospitality offered as part of Jael’s deception, which the song presents frankly to show how the mighty commander was overcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the word translated "butter" refers to curdled milk. Both traditions read the detail as heightening the irony of the scene: the warrior trusts a host’s hospitality and is undone by it.

verses.text: She put her hand to the tent peg, and her right hand to the workmen’s hammer. With the hammer she struck Sisera. She struck through his head. Yes, she pierced and struck through his temples.
verses.arminianNotes: She takes the tent peg and the workman’s hammer and strikes Sisera through the temples. Arminians read the stark description as the song’s way of showing the end of an oppressor, and they handle it with gravity rather than delight in the violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Tent work was often women’s work in that culture, so Jael uses tools she knew. Both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of Deborah’s word that the LORD would sell Sisera into a woman’s hand (4:9), with a sober view of the deed itself.

verses.text: At her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay. At her feet he bowed, he fell. Where he bowed, there he fell down dead.
verses.arminianNotes: At her feet he bowed, fell, and lay dead. Arminian readers see the repeated verbs slowing down the moment of his fall, showing the complete reversal of the proud commander who had oppressed Israel for twenty years (4:3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the deliberate repetition, which stresses the finality of his defeat. Both traditions read the verse as poetic emphasis on God humbling the oppressor, not as a call to dwell on the details of a death.

verses.text: “Through the window she looked out, and cried: Sisera’s mother looked through the lattice. ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why do the wheels of his chariots wait?’
verses.arminianNotes: Sisera’s mother looks through the lattice and asks why his chariot is so slow in coming. Arminians see the song turning to an enemy mother, which brings out the human cost of the war even as it shows the reversal of Sisera’s expectations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and observe the dramatic irony, since the reader knows Sisera is already dead. Interpreters differ on how much sympathy the scene evokes, and both traditions read it as heightening the reversal rather than mocking grief.

verses.text: Her wise ladies answered her, Yes, she returned answer to herself,
verses.arminianNotes: Her wise ladies answer her, and she answers herself too. Arminian readers see the self-reassurance of those who cannot imagine defeat, as Sisera’s household explains away the delay with the answer they want to hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the "wise" ladies’ answer proves foolish. Both traditions read the verse as showing how human confidence in military power deceives itself, setting up the closing prayer of 5:31.

verses.text: ‘Have they not found, have they not divided the plunder? A lady, two ladies to every man; to Sisera a plunder of dyed garments, a plunder of dyed garments embroidered, of dyed garments embroidered on both sides, on the necks of the plunder?’
verses.arminianNotes: The ladies imagine the army dividing plunder, a woman or two for every man and dyed embroidered garments for Sisera. Arminians read this as an exposure of the cruelty of Sisera’s war, in which captive women were counted as plunder, and see the song condemning that brutality.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony that those who expected to take captives have themselves been defeated. Both traditions read the verse as revealing the oppressor’s values and the justice of God’s judgment, not as an endorsement of plunder taking.

verses.text: “So let all your enemies perish, LORD, but let those who love him be as the sun when it rises in its strength.” Then the land had rest forty years.
verses.arminianNotes: The song ends praying that all the LORD’s enemies perish and that those who love him be like the sun rising in strength, and the land has rest forty years. Arminian readers see the final contrast between enemies and those who love the LORD as a call to choose love for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the prayer as confidence in God’s final justice and the flourishing of his people. Both traditions note that "forty years" of rest follows deliverance, as elsewhere in Judges (3:11), and see the rest as God’s gift.
